column1: # vendor-quirks.tsv — software known to trip Neptune's signature checks
# WHAT THIS IS: a labelling layer, not a suppression list. A finding that
# matches an entry here is still found, still listed, still counted, and still
# deducts from the score. All this adds is a name and a sentence, so that a
# first run on a working Mac reads as "six of these are Waves and Docker doing
# what they have always done" instead of eleven anonymous red lines.
# WHY NOT JUST ACKNOWLEDGE THEM: because that decision is not Neptune's to make.
# "Docker ships an unsigned root helper" is a fact about Docker. "That is fine
# on my machine" is a judgement about your threat model, and the cleaner
# products this tool was built to replace are precisely the ones that make it
# for you and call the result a clean bill of health. Acknowledging stays a
# thing you do deliberately, with --acknowledge, one finding at a time.
#   pattern  lowercase substring matched against the lowercased finding title.
#            Matched as a plain substring — no globs, no regex — so an entry
#   vendor   short name shown in the report
#   note     one sentence on what this software does and why it looks like this
# ADDING AN ENTRY: only for software whose behaviour you have actually verified
# on a machine, and only describing what it does — never asserting that it is
# safe. Every line here is a claim Neptune is making on the reader's behalf, so
# the bar is evidence, not plausibility.
# Entries are ordered most-specific first; the first match wins.

column3: Waves Audio ships WavesLocalServer, its licence and plugin-scanning daemon, without a valid signature. Longstanding across versions, and it listens only on localhost.
Waves Audio's local licence server. Unsigned in every shipped version to date; binds to 127.0.0.1 and [::1] only.
Waves Central's installer helper. Signed, but installs the unsigned components above.
SoundID Reference installs a system-wide audio agent. Some components are signed and some are not, in the same release.
SoundID Reference's system-wide audio processing agent, frequently shipped unsigned.
Docker Desktop's socket helper runs as root and ships unsigned. Docker's other helper, com.docker.vmnetd, is signed — the inconsistency is Docker's, not a sign of tampering.
PACE Anti-Piracy's licence daemon, bundled by most commercial audio plugins. Runs as root; the daemon binary is routinely unsigned while the framework beside it is signed.
PACE Anti-Piracy's licence daemon, installed by iLok-protected software. Runs as root and is routinely unsigned.
Elektron Overbridge installs a DriverKit extension and a launch agent for hardware audio devices.
Focusrite Control's server component, which listens on an all-interfaces port to talk to the audio interface.
Saffire MixControl's daemon for FireWire-era Focusrite hardware. Signed with a certificate that no longer carries a team ID.
Native Access and NI hardware services install several helpers; signing has been inconsistent across generations.
Arturia Software Center's updater agent and install helper.
Ableton Live's installer and index helpers.
Google's legacy updater. Its plists often outlive the binary they point at, which is why they show up as unresolvable rather than unsigned.
Google's current updater, installed by Chrome and other Google software.
Zoom's updater and its root daemon. Both signed; listed here because they are frequently queried.
Microsoft AutoUpdate, installed by any Office application.
Adobe's Creative Cloud helpers install several root daemons and launch agents.
Steam's cleanup agent.
The Epic Games launcher's login item.
